L02:
After 9 months and 3 teams, we've completed our migration from a monolith to microservices at our fintech.

The results: p99 latency down 40%. Deployments that used to take hours now take minutes. 3 teams shipping independently without stepping on each other.

The technical work turned out to be the easy part. The hard part was alignment — getting 3 teams to agree on service boundaries, ownership, and standards took more energy than any line of code.

My biggest lessons:
1. Start with the domain, not the technology.
2. Migrate incrementally — big bangs fail.
3. Celebrate small wins along the way.

To everyone who says microservices are overhyped: sometimes they're exactly the right tool for the job.

What's the biggest migration you've been part of?

L04:
In January, I was laid off from a big tech company.

Today, 6 months later, I've joined a 30-person startup to lead product.

The months in between were the hardest of my career. 200+ applications sent. Rejections. Interviews that went nowhere. Days where I questioned everything I thought I knew about my own value.

What I learned:
- Your job is not your identity.
- Rejection is redirection.
- The right opportunity is worth the wait.

To anyone navigating a layoff right now: the process is brutal, but you are not your job title, and this season will not last forever.

To the hiring managers who took the time to send thoughtful rejections — thank you. It mattered more than you know.

If you're job searching and need support, my DMs are open.
L05:
Most AI agent startups are thin wrappers around the same 3 foundation models.

Every week another "revolutionary AI agent" launches, and the pattern is the same: a clever prompt, a polished UI, and a foundation model doing all the heavy lifting underneath.

Prompts are not a moat. Anyone can copy them in an afternoon.

What actually creates defensibility:

Workflow depth — embedding so deeply into how a team works that switching becomes painful.

Proprietary data — feedback loops that make your product smarter every day.

The winners in this space won't be the ones with the best demo. They'll be the ones who understand their customers' workflows better than anyone else.

If you're building an AI agent startup, ask yourself one question: if the model providers shipped your feature tomorrow, what would be left?

Just wrapped a few days at SaaStr Annual. I met 40+ founders, sat in on dozens of sessions, and came away with 3 takeaways:

1. PLG is maturing. Product-led growth isn't just a buzzword anymore — companies are getting sophisticated about layering sales on top of self-serve motions.

2. AI pricing is unsettled. Nobody has cracked it. Seat-based? Usage-based? Outcome-based? Every founder I spoke with is experimenting, and not one of them sounded confident.

3. Community-led growth is back. After a few quiet years, community is everywhere again — but this time with real ROI expectations attached.

The energy in SaaS right now is unlike anything I've seen in years.

Were you at SaaStr? What was your biggest takeaway?
L07:
Roughly 70% of enterprise AI pilots never reach production.

It's not the models. The models are ready. They've been ready.

The real culprits:

1. Data readiness. Most enterprises are sitting on fragmented, inconsistent, poorly governed data. You can't build production AI on a foundation of spreadsheets and silos.

2. Missing process redesign. Too many companies bolt AI onto existing workflows and expect magic. AI doesn't just automate a process — it demands that you rethink it. Skip that step, and your pilot dies in the demo phase.

The companies succeeding with AI aren't the ones with the best models. They're the ones who did the unglamorous work first: cleaning their data, redesigning their processes, and preparing their people for change.

The technology isn't the bottleneck. We are.

If your organization is stuck between pilot and production, what's actually holding you back?

L09:
10 years in B2B sales, and the #1 skill isn't pitching, negotiating, or objection handling. It's listening.

A few years ago, I was on a call with a deal that was falling apart. The prospect had concerns, and every instinct told me to jump in with answers.

Instead, I shut up. For 90 full seconds.

The silence was excruciating. But in it, the prospect talked themselves through their own objection — and revealed the real blocker, one I never would have guessed.

We closed the deal two weeks later.

What a decade in sales taught me:
- Prospects will tell you exactly how to sell to them — if you let them.
- Silence isn't awkward. It's powerful.
- The best discovery question is sometimes no question at all.

Talk less. Sell more.

What's the best sales lesson you've learned the hard way?
L10:
After 3 years, I've made the hardest decision of my professional life: I'm shutting down Cartful.

We raised $1.1M. We grew to 4,000 users. We poured everything we had into this company. And we never found repeatable revenue.

Writing this is painful, but I owe it to everyone who believed in us to share what I learned.

Lesson 1: Users are not customers. We celebrated signups while avoiding the harder question: who will actually pay, and why?

Lesson 2: Repeatable revenue beats everything. One-off deals feel like traction. They're not. If you can't describe your sales motion in one sentence, you don't have one.

Lesson 3: Runway is for learning, not surviving. We stretched our runway to stay alive instead of spending it to find the truth faster.

To our investors, our team, and our users: thank you. I'm sorry we couldn't get there.

Failure isn't the opposite of success. It's tuition.
L11:
I stopped daily standups for my team of 14. The results surprised even me.

A few months ago, we replaced our daily standup with async written updates. Every morning, each person posts three things: what they did, what they're doing, and what's blocking them.

The results: 6 hours of meetings eliminated per week. Shipping speed completely unchanged. Engineers report fewer interruptions and more deep work.

Most standups aren't for the team. They're for the manager — a status ritual dressed up as collaboration.

Written updates turned out to be better in almost every way. People think before they write. Updates are searchable and permanent. Time zones stop mattering.

Standups aren't always wrong. But if your standup feels like a status meeting, it probably is one — and your team already knows it.

Would your team survive without daily standups?
L12:
I passed the AWS Solutions Architect Professional exam.

11 weeks of studying. A full-time job. 5 practice exams. Late nights and early mornings.

It's one of the hardest certifications I've pursued, and one of the most rewarding.

For anyone preparing for this exam, here's what worked for me:

- Consistency over intensity — one hour every day beats eight hours on Saturday.
- Practice exams are everything — I took 5, and each one exposed gaps I didn't know I had.
- Build, don't just read — hands-on labs made concepts stick in a way videos never could.
- Protect your study time like a meeting, because it is one.

To everyone balancing certifications with a full-time job: it's hard, but it's possible.

What certification are you working toward?
L13:
One year ago, I became an engineering manager. It's been the most humbling year of my career.

The hardest change wasn't the meetings, the 1:1s, or even the difficult conversations. It was learning to measure my output by my team's work — not my personal commits.

For years, my sense of accomplishment came from shipping code. Green squares. Merged PRs. Tangible progress I could point to at the end of every day.

Then my "output" became invisible. A good week meant my 7 direct reports were unblocked, growing, and shipping — while my own contributions showed up nowhere.

It took me months to stop feeling like an impostor.

What I learned in year one:
- Your team's success is your success.
- Most problems are communication problems in disguise.
- Clarity is the greatest gift a manager can give.
- Resist the urge to jump in and fix it yourself.

To every new EM struggling with the identity shift: you're not alone.

What was your hardest lesson as a first-time manager?
L14:
Documentation isn't glamorous. Nobody gets promoted for writing runbooks. But when our team of 9 SREs finally committed to them, on-call pages dropped 30% in a single quarter.

Not because our systems magically got better — because our knowledge stopped living exclusively in people's heads.

What we did:
- Every incident got a runbook entry, no exceptions.
- Every repeated page triggered a documentation review.
- We deleted outdated docs as aggressively as we wrote new ones.
- Runbook quality became part of our definition of done.

The ROI of documentation is invisible until you measure it: fewer 2 AM wake-ups, faster onboarding, less bus factor, calmer on-call rotations.

If your team is drowning in pages, don't buy another tool. Write a runbook.

How does your team approach documentation? I'd like to hear what's worked.
L15:
After 3 years fully remote, our company went hybrid — 2 days in the office.

The good: retention improved, and our numbers are better than they've been in two years. Onboarding got noticeably faster. Cross-team collaboration feels easier.

The hard: 2 senior people quit over the change — painful losses. Trust took a hit during the transition. And some days the office is half empty, and people wonder why they commuted.

There is no perfect answer to the remote vs hybrid debate. Every model has tradeoffs. Every policy will disappoint someone.

What matters is honesty. We told our team exactly why we made the change, and we accepted that some people would make a different choice for their lives. I respect that.

Anyone who claims remote vs hybrid is a solved problem is selling something.

What's your company's model — and is it actually working?
L16:
AI won't replace junior developers. But it will change what "junior" means.

We recently hired 2 junior engineers on my team. Both use AI pair-programming tools daily, and they ship production code faster than juniors did five years ago.

The skills that make them valuable have shifted. Less: memorizing syntax, writing boilerplate. More: reviewing code critically, asking the right questions, understanding systems.

The junior developer of today isn't someone who writes simple code slowly. It's someone who orchestrates AI tools, verifies their output, and learns architecture from day one.

The implications:
1. Hiring rubrics built around syntax trivia are obsolete.
2. Mentorship matters more, not less — judgment can't be autocompleted.
3. The ladder from junior to senior is compressing.

Companies that stop hiring juniors "because AI" aren't eliminating a cost. They're eliminating their future senior pipeline.

Are you still hiring junior devs? Why or why not?
L17:
Last week, a churned customer came back.

When they left, they told us the truth — our seat-based pricing punished them for growing their team. They were paying for licenses nobody used.

So we moved from seat-based to usage-based pricing. It was scary. We modeled the downside a dozen times. Some advisors told us not to do it.

Since the switch: expansion revenue is up 22%. Sales conversations start with value, not license counts. And churned customers are coming back on their own.

Pricing isn't just a revenue lever. It's a statement about whose side you're on. Seat-based pricing rewarded us when customers overbought. Usage-based pricing rewards us only when our customers succeed.

Aligning your incentives with your customers' is good ethics and good business.

Has your company changed its pricing model? What happened?

Six months ago, a bootcamp grad asked me to mentor them. This week, they signed an offer as a frontend developer at an insurance company.

The hard work was entirely theirs. I'm sharing this because the journey taught me as much as it taught them.

What we did over 6 months:
- Weekly check-ins, even when progress felt slow.
- Code reviews on real projects, not toy exercises.
- 4 mock interviews, each one harder than the last.
- Honest conversations about rejection and resilience.

Mentorship isn't about having all the answers. It's about being consistent when someone's confidence is wavering.

The tech industry loves to debate whether bootcamp grads can make it. With grit and the right support, they can.

If you're an experienced developer, mentor someone. One hour a week can change a career.

And to my mentee: congratulations. You earned every bit of this.
L19:
We changed one email subject line, and open rates jumped 31%.

For months, our emails to our 18k subscribers led with features: "New: Advanced Reporting Dashboard." Solid open rates. Nothing special.

Then we tried an experiment. Instead of describing the feature, we described the outcome — what the reader would actually get out of it.

Same email. Same list. Same send time. One change. Open rate up 31%.

The lesson is as old as marketing itself, but we needed the reminder: customers don't care about your features. They care about what your features do for them.

Feature-focused: "New: Advanced Reporting Dashboard"
Outcome-focused: "Find out where your pipeline is leaking"

One talks about you. The other talks about them.

Since then, we've rewritten every subject line in our lifecycle emails using the same principle, and the gains keep coming.

Audit your last 10 subject lines. How many talk about you vs your reader?
L20:
People often ask how our 12-person team stays productive without a big ops function. We run the entire company on 5 tools:

1. Linear — every task, bug, and project lives here. If it's not in Linear, it doesn't exist.
2. Notion — our company brain. Docs, wikis, meeting notes, onboarding.
3. Slack — communication, with strict channel hygiene to keep the noise down.
4. Figma — where every product idea becomes real before a single line of code is written.
5. Otto — our homegrown deploy bot. One command, and code goes from PR to production. Everyone's favorite teammate.

No sprawling tool stack. No overlapping subscriptions. No "wait, which doc is the source of truth?"

The principle behind it: every new tool adds a tax — context-switching, licenses, onboarding, integrations. We only add a tool when the pain of not having it exceeds that tax.

Simplicity is a competitive advantage.

What tools could your team not live without?
L21:
I just took my first real break in 4 years. Two weeks. No Slack. No email. No "quick calls."

The first few days were deeply uncomfortable. I checked my phone out of habit. I felt guilty. I convinced myself things would fall apart without me.

They didn't.

The real insight came when I returned. With fresh eyes, I could see how much of my busyness was self-inflicted. Within my first week back, I killed 3 recurring meetings that, it turns out, nobody missed.

What burnout taught me:
- Rest isn't a reward for finishing the work. The work is never finished.
- If your business can't survive 2 weeks without you, that's a design flaw, not a badge of honor.
- Exhaustion is not a personality trait.

To every founder and leader grinding without a break: the sabbatical you think you can't afford is probably the one you need most.

When was your last real break?

L23:
Networking events are mostly useless.

I used to attend every conference, every mixer, every "founder happy hour." I collected hundreds of business cards. Clients that came from all that networking: zero.

Meanwhile, my last 3 clients all came from the same place: writing online.

Why writing beats networking:
- Scale — a conversation reaches one person; a post reaches thousands.
- Selection — the right people come to you, already pre-sold on how you think.
- Compounding — a good post keeps working for months; a handshake is forgotten by Monday.

Networking events optimize for feeling productive. Writing optimizes for being findable.

Relationships still matter — they're everything. But the best ones start when someone reads your ideas and thinks, "this person gets it."

Stop collecting business cards. Start publishing your thinking. Your next client isn't at a conference. They're scrolling their feed.

I joined Supply Chain Weekly for episode 142 to talk about AI demand forecasting.

We covered why traditional forecasting methods break down in volatile markets, what AI-driven forecasting actually looks like in practice, and a real-world result: at one of our pilot customers, forecast error is down 18%.

We also got honest about the hard parts: data quality, change management, and why the forecasting team's expertise matters more with AI, not less.

Thank you to the hosts for the thoughtful questions.

Our year in review — the numbers, the wins, and the mistake I'd take back.

ARR: $1.2M to $3.4M
Team: 9 to 21
NPS: 61

By almost every measure, it was the best year in our company's history. But the metric I'm proudest of is that NPS — growth means nothing if customers don't love what you build.

My biggest mistake this year: hiring sales too early.

We brought on sales reps before we, the founders, had nailed the sales motion ourselves. The result: months of missed targets, frustrated reps, and expensive lessons. It wasn't their fault — it was mine. You can't hand off a playbook you haven't written.

We course-corrected, rebuilt the process from first principles, and things finally clicked. But I'd take those months back if I could.

I'm sharing this because year-in-review posts usually only show the highlight reel. Growth is messy.

What's your biggest lesson from this year?
